title: Controlled-Memory Identification with Shared Generators: Dimension--Horizon Tradeoffs and Quantum--Classical Separation
abstract: We determine the finite-horizon identification limits of a \(d\)-dimensional memory when the control interface is restricted to four shared, time-homogeneous generators. A writer encodes a message by applying a prefix word to a common root state. The verifier then applies a candidate-dependent query word followed by a shared terminal binary test, with each word of length at most \(T\). For fixed error tolerances \(λ_2>0\) and \(λ_1+λ_2<1\), the optimal identification sizes satisfy \(\ln N_{\mathsf Q,4}=Θ_{λ_1,λ_2}(\min\{d^2,T\})\) for arbitrary CPTP generators and \(\ln N_{\mathsf S,4}=Θ_{λ_1,λ_2}(\min\{d,T\})\) for stochastic maps. Four unitary letters and four permutation letters attain these respective bounds, showing that a four-letter reversible alphabet reaches the static code-size orders in optimal quadratic and linear word length. In the fully dimension-limited regime, this yields \(\ln N_{\mathsf Q,4}=Θ(d^2)\) versus \(\ln N_{\mathsf S,4}=Θ(d)\), establishing a quadratic quantum--classical separation in logarithmic code size. Low-overlap Grassmann and agreement-code packings supply the orbit endpoints, while exact inverse query words match each encoded state to its designated test. At the sharp boundary \(λ_2=0\), \(0\leqλ_1<1\), all four model classes satisfy \(\ln N=Θ(\min\{\ln d,T\})\). Thus any fixed positive false-acceptance tolerance activates the metric-packing regime, whereas zero false acceptance imposes an exclusive-witness constraint and yields the logarithmic-dimension boundary.
summary: This work establishes the fundamental limits on how much information can be reliably identified from a quantum or classical memory of dimension $d$ given a limited interaction budget $T$. It rigorously proves a quadratic quantum-classical separation in the required code size, showing that quantum systems can encode significantly more information than classical ones under these specific constraints.
main_problem: The paper determines the finite-horizon identification limits for encoding information about a $d$-dimensional memory using a restricted set of shared quantum or classical generators.
main_result: It establishes a quadratic quantum-classical separation in the logarithmic code size ($\Theta(d^2)$ vs. $\Theta(d)$) when considering fixed-error identification protocols.
method: The analysis involves optimizing the root state, terminal measurement, and generator set jointly by analyzing the structure of the resulting Hankel matrix, comparing finite-horizon bounds to static limits.
model_or_system: The model involves a two-phase identification protocol: a writer applies a prefix word to a root state, and a verifier applies a query word followed by a shared binary test. The system can be modeled by quantum channels (CPTP maps) or classical stochastic maps.
key_observables: The maximum achievable identification size, $N$, and its logarithmic scaling $\ln N$.
main_assumptions: The control interface is restricted to a small, fixed number (four) of shared, time-homogeneous generators.
paper_structure: The paper first formalizes the identification problem using dynamical systems and Hankel matrices. It then derives the finite-horizon bounds for quantum (CPTP/Unitary) and classical (Stochastic/Permutation) systems, highlighting the separation in the fully dimension-limited regime. Finally, it analyzes the distinct boundary conditions set by zero vs. positive false-acceptance tolerances.
why_interesting: The explicit quantum-classical separation in the scaling of information capacity ($\Theta(d^2)$ vs. $\Theta(d)$) provides a fundamental, resource-theoretic bound on quantum advantage in memory identification tasks.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Schematic dimension–horizon phase diagram. In panel (a), Q denotes the quantum/CPTP model and S denotes the classical/stochastic model. For fixed positive false-acceptance tolerance, the solid red curve is the quantum model and the dashed blue curve is the classical model; their laws are respectively Θ(min{d2, T}) and Θ(min{d, T}). At zero false acceptance, all four dynamical classes obey Θ(min{ln d, T}). The curves depict the asymptotic scaling orders; finite-dimensional constants are suppressed.
